question.text:
Consider the set $A = \{ p,m,o,q,r,s,t,u \}.$ Which subset must be placed into the blank in the set below so that it represents a partition of $A?$

\[ \{ \{ p,s \}, \{ t,o \}, \{ q,r \}, \, \_\_\_\_ \, \} \]
question.explanation:
A partition of a set $A$ is a collection of non-empty subsets of $A$ where every element of $A$ is contained in exactly one subset.

To find the subset that goes in the blank, we must identify which elements of $A$ are not yet contained within any of the given subsets.

Let's go through each element of $A$ and check:

  • $p \in \{ p,s \} \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

  • $m$ does not belong to any of the given subsets $\quad \color{red}\times$

  • $o \in \{ t,o \} \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

  • $q \in \{ q,r \} \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

  • $r \in \{ q,r \} \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

  • $s \in \{p,s \} \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

  • $t \in \{t,o \} \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

  • $u$ does not belong to any of the given subsets $\quad \color{red}\times$

The elements $m$ and $u$ are not yet contained within any of the given subsets. Therefore, the subset that must go in the blank is $\{ m,u \}.$

example.title: Identifying the Missing Set to Form a Partition

question.text: The function $f(x)$ is defined and differentiable on $[-5,5].$ The graph of $f'(x),$ the derivative of $f(x),$ is shown above, where the areas of the regions between the graph and the $x$-axis are $3,$ $9,$ and $2$ respectively (from left to right). Find the maximum value of $f(x)$ on the interval $[-5,5]$ given that $f(-5)=2.$
question.explanation:
According to the candidates test, the maximum value of $f(x)$ on $[-5,5]$ must occur at a critical point or an endpoint of the interval.

Step 1: Find the critical points:

We see that $f'(x)$ is defined everywhere on $x\in (-5,5),$ and $f'(x)=0$ at $x=-2, 3.$ Therefore, the candidates are $x=-5,-2,3,5.$

Step 2: Compute the value of $f$ for each candidate using the fundamental theorem of calculus:

Using the given information and the fundamental theorem of calculus, we have the following:

\begin{align*} f(-5) &= 2 \\[5pt] f(-2) &= f(-5) +\int_{-5}^{-2} f'(x)\,\textrm d x \\[5pt] &= 2 -3 \\[5pt] &=-1\\[5pt] f(3) &= f(-5) +\int_{-5}^{3} f'(x)\,\textrm d x \\[5pt] &= 2 -3+9 \\[5pt] &=8 \\[5pt] f(5) &= f(-5) +\int_{-5}^5 f'(x)\,\textrm d x \\[5pt] &= 2-3+9-2 \\[5pt] &=6 \end{align*}

Step 3: Select the largest value of $f$ from our candidates.

Comparing the values of $f$ found in step $2,$ we have \[ f_{\text{max}} = \max\{2,-1, 8,6\} = 8. \]

Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is $f_{\text{max}}=8,$ and the value of $x$ that maximizes $f(x)$ is $x_\text{max}=3.$

question.text:
The functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are twice-differentiable on an open interval containing $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$ The values of $f,$ $g,$ and their respective derivatives are given below:

$x$ $f(x)$ $f'(x)$ $f''(x)$ $g(x)$ $g'(x)$ $g''(x)$
$\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ $1$ $1$ $4$ $0$ $0$ $-2$
\[\]

Find $\lim\limits_{x \to \left(\pi/2\right)} \dfrac{\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)-f(x)}{g(x)}.$
question.explanation:
Notice that if we try to substitute $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ directly into the limit, we reach the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0}.$ \begin{align*} \lim\limits_{x \to \left(\pi/2\right)} \dfrac{\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) - f(x)}{g(x)-\cos(2x)} & = \left.\dfrac{\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) - f(x)}{g(x)}\right|_{x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\tan \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) - f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)}{g\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1-1}{0} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{0}{0} \end{align*}

So, we use L'Hopital's rule: \begin{align*} \lim\limits_{x \to \left(\pi/2\right)} \dfrac{\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)-f(x)}{g(x)} & = \lim\limits_{x \to \left(\pi/2\right)} \dfrac{\left(\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)-f(x)\right)'}{(g(x))'} \\[5pt] & = \lim\limits_{x \to \left(\pi/2\right)} \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) - f'(x)}{g'(x)} \end{align*}

We substitute $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ again, but once more, we reach the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0}.$ \begin{align*} \lim\limits_{x \to \left(\pi/2\right)} \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) - f'(x)}{g'(x) } & = \left. \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) - f'(x)}{g'(x) } \right|_{x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}\sec^2 \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) - f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)}{g'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1-1}{0 } \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{0}{0} \end{align*}

We apply L'Hopital's rule again. We get \begin{align*} \lim\limits_{x \to \left(\pi/2\right)} \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) - f'(x)}{g'(x)} & = \lim\limits_{x \to \left(\pi/2\right)} \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) - f'(x)\right)'}{(g'(x) )'} \\[5pt] &= \lim\limits_{x \to \left(\pi/2\right)} \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) - f''(x)}{g''(x)}, \end{align*}

and this time, when we substitute $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2},$ we are actually able to determine the result: \begin{align*} \lim\limits_{x \to \left(\pi/2\right)} \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) - f''(x)}{g''(x)} & = \left. \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) - f''(x)}{g''(x) } \right|_{x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}\sec^2 \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\tan \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) - f''\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)}{g''\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot 1 - 4}{(-2)} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2} \end{align*}

Therefore, $\lim\limits_{x \to \left(\pi/2\right)} \dfrac{\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)-f(x)}{g(x)-\cos(2x)} = \dfrac{3}{2}.$

question.text:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the graph of the function $y=f(x)$ shown above?

  1. ${\displaystyle \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{ f(h) -f(0)}{h}=-1} $
  2. ${\displaystyle \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{ f(2+h) -f(2)}{h} =0}$
  3. ${\displaystyle \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{ f(3+h) -f(3)}{h} =1.5}$
question.explanation:
Comparing these limits with the formula for the instantaneous rate of change

\[ f'(a) = \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}, \] we see that

\begin{align*} \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{ f(h) -f(0)}{h} &= f'(0),\\[5pt] \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{ f(2+h) -f(2)}{h} &= f'(2),\\[5pt] \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{ f(3+h) -f(3)}{h} &= f'(3). \end{align*}

The function consists of two line segments. Inspecting the graph, we see that

  • for $x < 2$, we have $f'(x)=0.5,$

  • for $x>2$, we have $f'(x)=1.5.$

The derivative does not exist at $x=2.$ So, we have

\begin{align*} \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{ f(h) -f(0)}{h} &= 0.5, \\[5pt] \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{ f(2+h) -f(2)}{h} &=\text{DNE}, \\[5pt] \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{ f(3+h) -f(3)}{h} &=1.5. \end{align*}

Therefore, only statement III is true.

question.explanation:
Recall that \begin{align} \newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits} \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d z}(\csch z) = -\csch{z}\coth z & \quad\Rightarrow\quad \int \csch{z}\coth{z} \, \textrm dz = -\csch{z} + C,\\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d z}(\tanh z) = \sech^2{z} & \quad\Rightarrow\quad \int \sech^2{z} \, \textrm dz = \tanh{z} + C. \end{align}

Therefore, we have \begin{align} \int (\sech^2 z + \csch{z}\coth{z} ) \, \textrm{d}z &=\int \sech^2 z \, \textrm{d}z + \int \csch{z}\coth{z} \, \textrm{d}z\\[5pt] & = \tanh{z} -\csch{z} + C. \end{align}

question.text: The graph of the function $y = g(x)$ is shown above. Approximate $g'(x)$ at the point $x=3$ using a central difference approximation with step size $h=1.$
question.explanation: We use the central difference approximation \[ g'(x) \approx \frac{g(x+h) - g(x-h)}{2h}, \] at the point $x = 3$ with step size $h=1.$ This gives \begin{align*} g'(3) &\approx \frac{g(3+1) - g(3-1)}{2}\\[5pt] &=\frac{g(4) - g(2)}{2}\\[5pt] &=\frac{1-4}{2}\\[5pt] &=-\frac{3}{2}\\[5pt] &=-1.5. \end{align*}
